The claim you already have, from his April 10, 2018 Senate hearing that AI tools for spotting hate speech were 5 to 10 years away, still stands. But I couldn't re-quote it: the Wikisource transcript I opened cuts off just before his answer.

- **Searches:** I ran the three fixed searches exactly as written, once each. They returned only recent coverage (2024–2026) and nothing said in 2018. I then ran six searches aimed at that year's events, so 9 of the 12 were used.
- **Page openings: all six used, and only one gave me text.** A bug in my own code threw away the text of the first five pages I opened. They were the Senate transcript, the April 2018 and October 2018 earnings-call transcripts, the November 15, 2018 press-call transcript, and the Washington Post transcript of the House hearing. That bug also made me open the Senate transcript a second time, which used up the sixth opening. That second copy (about 34,000 characters) ends before his answer to Senator Thune on hate speech. **I read none of the other four pages and quote nothing from them.**
- **Leads seen only in search snippets (not quotable):**
  - Coverage of the April 25 earnings call reports him saying AI finds nudity more easily than hate speech, with no date given.
  - His November 15, 2018 post, "A Blueprint for Content Governance and Enforcement," is about using AI to remove harmful content before anyone reports it. I didn't open it, so I can't say whether it names a date.
  - His other 2018 interviews and talks were not searched.
- **Ruled out:** the "by the end of this year… more than 20,000 people" pledge in the hearing coverage is about hiring staff, so it is a business forecast, not an AI prediction.
